raw_transcript:
So. This is the churn dashboard thing. It's, uh, Monday afternoon, October 19th. I'm gonna ramble, sorry future me.

Background: Dana Whitlock, who runs customer success at Brightfold, asked us two weeks ago why the churn rate on the Looker, uh, not Looker, on the Quill dashboard jumped from 4.1 percent to 6.8 percent in September. And everyone kind of panicked. Marcus Teague, my manager, wanted an answer by this Friday, the 23rd, for the leadership review.

So what I found. It's, it's mostly not real churn. The September number includes accounts that were migrated from the old billing system to the new one, and during migration, um, the old account IDs got closed and new ones opened, and the churn query counts a closed account as churned. I joined the churned accounts against the migration log and 1,240 of the, let me look, 1,912 churned accounts in September have a matching new account opened within 7 days. Within 7 days. So if you exclude those, the real number is 672 churned accounts, and the churn rate goes to, I calculated, 2.4 percent. Hmm, wait, that seems low. Let me redo it. Total active at start of September was 28,100. 672 over 28,100 is, um, 2.39, so yes, 2.4 percent. Which is actually lower than August's 4.1. Which is weird, and makes me suspicious. August might also have had migrations, the migration started August 20th. So August is probably inflated too. I haven't checked August yet. That's the honest state.

I talked to Femi Adesanya on the data engineering side, he owns the billing pipeline, and he confirmed that the migration closes the old account with status "closed" instead of a separate "migrated" status. He said adding a migrated status is maybe a sprint of work and is not on their roadmap. So, for now, the fix has to be in our query.

Um, side note, the BigQuery bill for this month is going to be ugly, I ran the full-history join like six times because I kept forgetting to add the partition filter. Something like 4 terabytes scanned. Not proud.

What I actually built: a dbt model, it's called fct_churn_adjusted, which excludes accounts with a matching new account within 7 days. I wrote two dbt tests, one for uniqueness of account_id and one that the adjusted count is never higher than the raw count. Both pass. But I have not deployed the model to production dbt, it's only in my dev schema. And I did not change the Quill dashboard, because Dana's team uses it daily and Marcus said not to touch it until leadership agrees on the definition.

I also, I started a writeup, a two-page doc, but it's maybe half done. The recommendation section is empty.

Uncertainty, um, the 7 day window is arbitrary. I picked 7 because most migrations matched within 2 days, but some took 5. Femi thinks some enterprise accounts took up to 3 weeks. If we used 21 days the adjusted churn might be even lower, I don't know, I didn't run it.

Next steps. Check August with the same logic. Run the 21 day sensitivity. Finish the writeup by Wednesday so Marcus can review Thursday before the Friday meeting. And, um, add the partition filter. Seriously.

Oh, and one more thing, Dana pinged me at like 5 pm asking if she can just tell her team that churn is "fine". And I said, um, please don't, not yet, because I haven't checked August and the definition isn't agreed. I said she could say the September spike is mostly a measurement artifact from the migration, that's fair, that part I'm fairly confident in, maybe 85 percent. She was okay with that. I also need to, uh, to remember that the finance team has their own churn number, from the revenue side, and it's computed totally differently, revenue churn versus logo churn. If leadership puts those side by side it's going to be confusing. I should add a paragraph on that to the writeup. Right, and Marcus asked for a chart with both raw and adjusted lines by month for the whole year. I haven't built that, it depends on the August check anyway.
